title: Canary Signal Conductor — notes & steward runbook (working)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch for a small, low-friction operational surface we call the "Signal Conductor" — a cross-functional lightweight orchestration and decision layer for canaries and A/B runs that emphasizes observable safety, cost-aware exposure and fast human-in-the-loop decisions.

Audience:
- Product and release leads running LLM feature experiments
- Runbook stewards (oncall or designated rollout owners)
- SRE/Observability and Solutions Eng who implement telemetry and fallback hooks

Why a "Conductor" concept?
- Problem: canaries produce many noisy signals across cost, latency, model quality and safety. Teams default to either too many manual checks or to a single blunt SLA (e.g., latency 95p).
- Goal: centralize signal harmonization and escalation choreography so small teams can run safer, faster rollouts without a heavy schedule or heavyweight gating process.

High-level primitives (v0):
1) Signal roster (live): prioritized list of signals (each with owner and threshold state). Example signals: latency P95, request error rate, per-token cost delta, rerank precision lift, hallucination/TOXicity alerts (human-review hit rate), semantic-drift score vs control embeddings.
2) Steward role: designated human responsible for decisions during the rollout window. (15–60 minute response SLA).
3) Conductor policy: a policy file that maps signal state -> actions (hold, slow-expose, continue, full-stop, automatic-fallback). Start conservative: on 2 independent medium signals or 1 high signal -> stop.
4) Observation window: canonicalize to 5m buckets for short canaries, 1h for longer staged exposures.
5) Escalation choreography: who to ping and how (Slack channel, oncall, pager, and a short decision checklist).

Quick runbook (operator checklist) — pre-flight (before exposure):
- Confirm steward assignment and second (backup) steward.
- Verify experiment config: cohort size, routing rule, fallback model/version, start/end times.
- Validate telemetry pipelines: ensures latency, error-rate, cost, quality signals are wired and green. Run smoke queries: "SELECT count(*) FROM canary_events WHERE _route = 'my-canary' AND ts > now()-15m" (placeholder).
- Confirm synthetic probes are running (canonical prompts for safety and quality checks).
- Set slack channel with pinned experiment summary and quick links (dashboards, logs, rollback playbook).
- Quick cost guard: estimate worst-case QPS * expected tokens * per-token-cost -> cap for the first hour.

During exposure (first 60 min):
- Check cadence: minute 0, 5, 15, 30, 60 (automatic snapshots + steward reviews).
- If any "high" severity signal triggers: initiate full-stop and run immediate rollback.
- If "medium" signals: consider slow-expose (reduce cohort by factor of 2 or drop QPS), require steward confirmation to continue.
- If signals are all "green": continue to scheduled expansion.

Signal severity heuristics (suggested) — start conservative and tune:
- High: latency P95 increase > 2x baseline AND error-rate increase > 0.5pp absolute OR safety human-review hit rate > 1%
- Medium: latency P95 increase 30–100% OR cost per-request increase > 30% OR semantic-drift score shift > threshold T (see telemetry)
- Low: small statistical blips; track but do not gate.

Cohort selection heuristics (to reduce confounders):
- Prefer orthogonal cohorts: pick a dimension that doesn’t correlate with peak load (e.g., account-created-before-date vs geography). Avoid time-of-day slices for first canaries.
- Keep at least two control subgroups if doing multi-arm (A/B/C) to enable pairwise checks.
- Synthetic traffic to baseline models should be interleaved to detect regression in routing and caching.

Telemetry checklist (minimum signals to implement before using conductor):
- Latency P50/P95/P99, per-route and per-model.
- Request error count and error categories (timeout, bad-request, inference-fail).
- Token counts (input and output) per request and aggregated per-minute.
- Cost estimate metric (tokens * model unit cost) aggregated per cohort.
- Quality proxies: rerank nDCG, BLEU/ROUGE or prompt-specific eval metrics, embedding drift (cosine distance distribution).
- Safety proxies: automated safety classifier hit-rate, human-review hit queue length and rate.
- Observability: request sample capture (with PII redaction), trace id linking to logs and model versions.

Fallback and automated actions (examples):
- Soft-fallback: route to cheaper quantized variant when cost increases beyond guardrail but latency OK.
- Hard-fallback: route to control model/version on high-severity signal.
- Slow-expose: reduce exposure by no more than one halving step every 15 minutes unless steward authorizes larger jump.

Escalation messages (template snippets):
- Auto message (Slack): "[CONDUCTOR][my-canary] HIGH LATENCY P95 (>2x) detected at 14:05 UTC. Auto-stop triggered. Steward: @Priya. Links: dashboard | rollback-playbook | traces. Please acknowledge."
- Steward checklist when acknowledging: 1) confirm signal is valid (no instrumentation regression), 2) check sample traces for root cause, 3) decide rollback vs slow-expose, 4) communicate to stakeholders.

Post-stop diagnostics quick list:
- Check autoscaling spikes and GPU saturation metrics.
- Inspect model load distribution and cache hit rates.
- Sample 50 failed requests and 50 successful control requests for quick manual review.
- If safety-related, freeze any expansion and start human-review queue triage (SLA: 2 hours).

Decision matrix (compact):
- Latency P95 high + errors high -> STOP + hard-fallback + SRE investigation.
- Cost high only -> SOFT-FALLBACK to quantized model + reduce cohort.
- Quality regressions small but non-zero -> PAUSE EXPANSION + additional evals on representative prompt set.
- Safety hit -> STOP + escalate to Product Safety + legal if required.

Operational automations we should build (v1 backlog):
- Signal weighter: compute a single summary health score tuned per-product via configurable weights.
- Canary simulator: run offline synthetic replay against candidate model to estimate signal distributions prior to exposure.
- One-click rollback that tags telemetry and marks experiment as "rolled back" in experiment ledger.
- Slack manifest auto-generation with required links and steward/backup.

Open questions / trade-offs (to discuss with team):
- How many simultaneous canaries should a steward reasonably own? (Tradeoff: familiarity vs burnout.)
- What is the right cadence for expanding cohorts in high-load products? (15m vs 1h vs 6h)
- Should we allow automated expansion beyond first hour if signals are all green? Who signs off?
- When is statistical significance required for quality metrics vs pragmatic operational gating?

Immediate next steps (this doc owner + collaborators):
- Wire a minimal telemetry set into dev dashboard for the next canary (Ethan).
- Draft a simple conductor policy schema (JSON) with our initial severity rules (Marta).
- Run a tabletop exercise with SRE and Solutions Eng to validate escalation messages (Liu).

Notes-to-self / fragments:
- We should keep the conductor policy human-readable at first and then codify.
- Consider a "gray-route" concept where uncertain traffic is 1% duplicated to both control and candidate (non-activated) to get exact diff signal.
- If we auto-fallback, log and tag the customer request ids so downstream teams can reproduce.

Appendix: quick example policy snippet (human-readable):
- "if latency_p95_ratio > 2 and error_rate_delta > 0.5pp -> action: hard-fallback, notify: sres, steward"
- "if cost_delta > 30% and latency_ok -> action: soft-fallback to quantized, throttle exposure by 50%"

End of working notes.
Please add comments inline and put proposed edits in the "conductor-policy-v1" branch in the rollout-scripts repo.
